headline: Six papers claim exact critical laws for the planar XY model, as the Berezinskii–Kosterlitz–Thouless picture predicts.
scope: The nearest-neighbor cosine XY model on the square lattice, its critical point and approach to it, plus discrete Gaussian height models.
plain: In the XY model, needles on a grid prefer to point the same way. Physicists predicted exact laws for how alignment fades at and near the critical point. These papers claim to prove them: the critical power 1/4, with a logarithmic correction, and the predicted law for the fading length near the threshold. Two of the papers depend on stated inputs from the others.
doesNot: This does not compute the constants in these laws, and two results rest on stated inputs from companion papers.
origin: This result comes from an unreleased OpenAI model, published in the openai/math release on 6 October 2026.

scorecard.significanceWhy: It would turn central predictions of the Berezinskii–Kosterlitz–Thouless theory into theorems for the standard XY model.

explanation:
Put a compass needle at each point of a flat square grid. Each needle can point in any direction in the plane. Neighbors prefer to point the same way, with a strength b, weighted by e raised to b times the cosine of the angle between them. This is the XY model[1]. The question is how strongly two needles r steps apart stay aligned on average.

At the critical strength, the answer claimed here is a constant times r^(−1/4)·(log r)^(1/8)[2]. Take r = 100 and then r = 10,000. The plain power r^(−1/4) shrinks by a factor of about 0.316. The logarithm factor grows by 2^(1/8), about 1.090. Together the alignment shrinks by a factor of about 0.345. The logarithm is a small correction, but it never goes away[3].

This model has a famous transition. Berezinskii predicted in 1971 that alignment fades slowly, like a power of distance, at low temperature[4]. Kosterlitz and Thouless explained the transition by swirls of needles, called vortices, that pair up or come loose[5]. Above the critical temperature, alignment fades exponentially. Below it, it fades like a power. Physicists predicted that, exactly at the switch, the power is 1/4[6]. They also predicted a strange law for the fading length near the switch.

Rigorous work confirmed parts of the picture. McBryan and Spencer proved power-law upper bounds[7]. Fröhlich and Spencer proved the low-temperature phase with slow fading exists[8]. Van Engelenburg and Lis proved a power-law lower bound at the threshold, but not with the sharp power[9].

The six papers claim to settle several predictions. One claims the critical power is exactly 1/4[10]. Another claims the logarithmic correction above, with a positive constant[2]. A third claims the predicted law for the fading length ξ near the threshold. As the strength b rises toward its critical value, the square root of the gap times log ξ tends to a positive constant[11]. So ξ grows like e raised to a constant over that square root. As an illustration with constant 1, a gap of 0.04 gives a length near 148. A gap of 0.01 gives a length near 22,000. The real constant is not computed. A fourth paper claims the large-scale random heights of a related model look like a Gaussian field, with a universal critical value[12].

Two papers rest on stated inputs from their companions. One claims the alignment at the center of a square with fixed boundary needles[13]. It assumes stated inputs from the companion papers[13]. The other claims the limit of the whole needle field at the critical point[14]. It uses the companion theorems on heights and pins[14].

The single obstacle is that the transition is very gentle. Near it, standard methods see only slow, logarithmic changes. The papers work through a dual description by random integer heights[15]. Earlier work with these heights did not pin down the exact constant at the threshold or its power[15].

How sure is this? There is no Lean formalization for these results in the openai/math release, so no computer has checked the proofs. Two of the six papers depend on stated inputs from the others. The constants in the main formulas are shown to exist but are not computed. No specialist review of any of the papers has been published.
hypeCheck: Major if it holds. There is no Lean check, two papers rest on stated companion inputs, the constants are not computed, and no specialist review is published.

glossary.meaning: A grid of planar needles, where neighbors prefer to point the same way.
The coupling strength b_c where fading switches from exponential to power-law.
The distance over which alignment fades by a fixed factor in the exponential regime.
A spot around which the needles turn through a full circle.
An extra factor that grows like a power of log r, slower than any power of r.
A standard random surface whose heights have a bell-curve law at every point.
A random surface with integer heights at each grid point, linked to the XY model by duality.

claims.sourceQuote: The planar XY model at inverse temperature \(b>0\), with free boundary, is the probability measure \begin{equation}\label{eq:xy-law} \frac{1}{Z_{R,b}} \exp\left\{b\sum_{\{x,y\}\in E_R}\cos(\theta_x-\theta_y)\right\} \prod_{x\in\Lambda_R}\frac{\dd\theta_x}{2\pi}, \qquad \theta_x\in\R/(2\pi\Z). \end{equation}
